grade.first_issue: The first decisive defect is the claimed bound that every inclusion-minimal hitting set of \(\mathcal G_n\) has size at most \(|\mathcal P(a_1)|\) merely because \(\mathcal P(a_1)\) is itself a hitting set. This implication is false in general and does not establish the bounded-rank premise needed for stabilization. Thus the central stabilization argument is unsupported, invoking Rule E and capping the score at 3.
grade.summary: The hitting-set reformulation is useful, and a stabilized finite family would indeed yield a periodic set of admissible integers. However, the proof of stabilization—the heart of the problem—rests on false set-theoretic assertions. Moreover, the final passage from eventual periodicity to periodicity for every index does not establish the necessary index alignment. Repairing the central argument requires a genuinely new finiteness argument comparable in substance to the reference solution.
strengths: Correctly reformulates the gcd conditions as a hitting-set condition on prime supports.

Correctly observes that, conditional on stabilization to a finite family \(\mathcal G\), membership in the resulting admissible set is periodic modulo the product of the primes in \(\bigcup\mathcal G\).
The resulting eventual recurrence for the increasing enumeration of that periodic set is essentially correct.

errors.description: A known hitting set of size \(m\) does not bound the sizes of all inclusion-minimal hitting sets. For example, the intersecting family \(\{\{p,q_i\}:1\le i\le r\}\) has the hitting set \(\{p\}\), while \(\{q_1,\ldots,q_r\}\) is an inclusion-minimal hitting set of arbitrarily large size.

The assertion that every \(S\in\mathcal G_n\) is a minimal hitting set of \(\mathcal G_{n-1}\) is false even for admissible sequences. If \(a_1=10\), then \(a_2=12\), and \(\mathcal G_2=\{\{2,5\},\{2,3\}\}\); neither two-element set is an inclusion-minimal hitting set of \(\mathcal G_1=\{\{2,5\}\}\).

The cited claim that bounded-rank intersecting families have only finitely many isomorphism classes is false: the star families \(\{\{p,q_i\}:1\le i\le r\}\) already give infinitely many nonisomorphic rank-two examples. Consequently, the claimed stabilization of \(\mathcal G_n\) is not proved. A decreasing density bounded below would not by itself imply stabilization either.

Even assuming stabilization, eventual enumeration of \(C\) does not by itself imply \(a_n=c_{j+n-1}\) for all large \(n\); there could be a persistent index offset. The submitted propagation argument only carries strict inequality forward and never contradicts an established equality at \(N\). Thus the required all-index conclusion is not proved as written, triggering the quantifier concern of Rule D.
